phonemes.desc: Palato-alveolar affricate [tʃ], as in English 'chin'. The initial cluster is a common Murrinh-Patha orthographic convention for a single consonant sound.
Short vowels [i] and [ɪ] alternating in an unstressed syllable sequence; Murrinh-Patha is stress-timed, with vowel quality governed by syllable position.
Final [m] and [n] are plain bilabial and alveolar nasals; the name ends in a closed syllable common in Murrinh-Patha proper names.

pronunciation.approximation: 'CHIN-ih-min' — stress the first syllable, keep the vowels short and clear, and pronounce the initial 'tj' as English 'ch'.

kin.label: Murrinh-Patha
kin.form: Tjinimin — the ancestral being who appears in Murrinh-Patha Dreaming narratives collected by W. E. H. Stanner.

kin.label: English gloss
kin.form: No transparent English etymology; the name is treated as a proper noun for an ancestral figure.

pronunciation.note: The PuniCodex lexicon classifies Tjinimin as 'Trickster, Moth Man', but the published Murrinh-Patha sources associate the figure with the bat (flying fox) and the Rainbow Serpent Kunmanggur. The 'moth' label is not attested in the scholarly record and should be treated as provisional. Because the name is already written in basic Latin letters, the Unicode restoration capitalizes the initial letter only; no diacritic or original-script mark is recovered. The entry is therefore Tier 2.

domains.title: Ancestor of the Peoples
domains.subtitle: Bat, Rainbow Serpent, and Ancestral Law
domains.lead: Tjinimin is an ancestral being in the mythology of the Murrinh-Patha peoples of the Daly River region, Northern Territory. He is remembered as an ancestor of the Australian peoples, closely associated with the bat or flying fox and with Kunmanggur, the great Rainbow Serpent. His story turns on a quarrel, a vow, and the origin of the bat's short nose — a narrative that encodes law, social restraint, and the place of humans within the Dreaming.

cards.name: Ancestry
cards.desc: Tjinimin is identified in Murrinh-Patha tradition as an ancestor of the Australian peoples, a foundational figure in the genealogical memory of the Daly River communities.

cards.name: Bat and Flying Fox
cards.desc: The figure is associated with the bat; a key myth explains the bat's short nose as the result of Tjinimin's vow and transformation.

cards.name: Rainbow Serpent
cards.desc: Tjinimin's narrative is bound to Kunmanggur, the Rainbow Serpent, whose consorts and authority set the moral stakes of the story.

cards.name: Trickster and Law
cards.desc: His attempt to transgress social boundaries, his defeat, and his lasting vow form a cautionary tale about desire, consequence, and the establishment of ancestral law.

symbols.name: Bat or flying fox
symbols.meaning: The animal form and kinship emblem linked to Tjinimin; the myth of the short nose explains the bat's distinctive face.

symbols.name: Rainbow Serpent (Kunmanggur)
symbols.meaning: The great water-spirit and law-giver whose authority Tjinimin challenges; the serpent marks the boundary between acceptable and forbidden desire.

symbols.name: The upside-down tree
symbols.meaning: The place where Tjinimin hung after his defeat, looking at the stars and making his vow of abstinence.

symbols.name: Stars
symbols.meaning: The night sky that Tjinimin contemplated while suspended; a symbol of reflection, withdrawal, and transformation.

mythology.lead: The principal Murrinh-Patha narrative of Tjinimin, recorded by W. E. H. Stanner, is a compact myth of boundary-crossing and transformation. It explains kinship, animal form, and the moral order through a single ancestral episode.

myths.title: The Quarrel with Kunmanggur
myths.text: Tjinimin quarrelled with Kunmanggur, the great Rainbow Serpent. He desired Kunmanggur's consorts, the Green Parrot-Girls, and sought to take them for himself. The dispute set the ancestral being against the authority of the Rainbow Serpent, testing the limits of proper relationship and social order.

myths.title: The Vow beneath the Stars
myths.text: Defeated in the quarrel, Tjinimin hung himself upside down in a tree. There he gazed at the stars and made a solemn vow: he would never have sex again. The posture of suspension and the vow of abstinence mark a radical withdrawal from the social and reproductive world.

myths.title: The Short Nose of the Bat
myths.text: Soon after his vow, Tjinimin's nose fell off. The myth explains this as the reason bats in the region have short noses: the ancestral being's bodily transformation became the permanent form of the animal with which he is associated. What began as social conflict ended as biological signature.

syncretism: Tjinimin belongs specifically to Murrinh-Patha tradition rather than to the wider cross-cultural networks of the Kimberley Wandjina or Arnhem Land Rainbow Serpent complexes. Within Murrinh-Patha cosmology he is grouped with the ancestor-figures whose stories encode law, kinship, and the origins of animal species. Comparative scholarship sometimes links him to the broader Australian theme of the Moon-Man or to nocturnal transformation myths, but these connections remain speculative; the primary attested context is the Daly River region.
culturalLegacy: Tjinimin survives in Murrinh-Patha oral tradition, initiation teaching, and the ethnographic record compiled by W. E. H. Stanner and later scholars. The story is used in initiation contexts to instruct young men in ancestral law, social restraint, and the consequences of transgression. Unlike the widely commercialised Wandjina imagery of the Kimberley, Murrinh-Patha sacred narratives such as that of Tjinimin are generally restricted to initiated custodians and are not reproduced as open visual art.
extendedMeditation:
Tjinimin is a difficult ancestor because his story turns on failure rather than triumph. He desires what is not his, loses, withdraws, and is transformed. The myth does not celebrate his ambition; it records the cost of transgression and the permanent mark it leaves on the body. In this he is close to the trickster type, but he is also a cautionary figure: the ancestor whose own choice limits him.

For contemporary readers, Tjinimin raises questions about the relationship between desire and law. What does it mean to make a vow that cannot be undone? How does a community remember the one who overreached and was changed? The bat's short nose is not merely an etiological detail; it is a material reminder that ancestral actions continue to shape the living world.
originalScriptNote: No indigenous writing system is securely attested for Murrinh-Patha proper names in the pre-contact period. The name Tjinimin appears in scholarly transcription using the Latin alphabet, with tj representing a palato-alveolar affricate. The PuniCodex restoration capitalises the initial letter; the ASCII form tjinimin is otherwise identical. Because no diacritic, stress mark, or original-script character is recoverable, the name is classified as Tier 2.

etymology.derivation: The name is a Murrinh-Patha proper noun; its internal etymology is not transparent in the published scholarly record. It is preserved as the name of an ancestral being associated with the bat and the Rainbow Serpent Kunmanggur.

nameVariations.note: Standard scholarly transcription used by W. E. H. Stanner and later sources.

archaeology: No fixed archaeological site is publicly identified with Tjinimin. Murrinh-Patha sacred geography is held by custodians and is not published in open scholarly form. The primary 'site' of the narrative is the Daly River country of the Northern Territory, where the story is maintained through initiation, ceremony, and oral transmission.
